title: Price controls

definition.text: Government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services in a market.

facts.text: There are two main kinds: a price ceiling sets the most that may be charged and a price floor the least; rent control and the minimum wage are well-known examples.
They aim to keep goods affordable during shortages, slow inflation, or guarantee a minimum income to some providers.
Price controls are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders, and Diocletian tried to cap the price of every commodity in the late 3rd century AD, with little success.
Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, causing shortages, and shortages feed black markets with higher prices.
During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry.
Western economists generally hold that consumer price controls fail, though since the 1990s minimum wages have won strong support among some economists.
Price controls are one of the indirect ways governments subsidise energy.

contested_note: Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, while some support minimum wages and other price caps.

definition.text: A pricing strategy in which the same seller charges different buyers different prices for the same or nearly the same good, according to which group they seem to belong to.

facts.text: It works by exploiting differences in buyers' willingness to pay and in how sensitive they are to price.
The seller needs market power; otherwise buyers would switch sellers or resell cheap units to those charged more.
In first-degree, or perfect, price discrimination each buyer pays their maximum, so the seller captures all consumer surplus.
Second-degree discrimination varies price with the quantity bought; third-degree charges different groups different prices, as with student and senior discounts.
The aim is to raise profit by shifting consumer surplus to the seller.
Drug-makers charge more in wealthier countries; antiretroviral drugs cost far less in Africa, where sales would otherwise be very limited.
The first-, second- and third-degree categories are attributed to Pigou.
